The Shell Bottleneck Has Not Reached the Chemistry Yet

Western artillery rearmament is usually presented as a race to build more shell factories. That framing is incomplete, but it is not yet wrong.

By Bottleneck Briefs · Published 2026-06-21 · Updated 2026-06-28 · 11 min read

In brief

  • 36,000 rounds/month was completed U.S. 155mm output in March 2026.
  • Projectile metal parts, not energetics, are the demonstrated current U.S. constraint.
  • 5 million lb/year is Graham’s awarded domestic TNT capability.
  • 2027–2029 is the likely window for an upstream energetics squeeze.

The current bottleneck is still visible metal

The U.S. Army missed its October 2025 objective of producing 100,000 completed 155mm rounds per month. A July 2026 Defense Department Inspector General evaluation reported completed-round output of approximately 36,000 per month as of March 2026, a figure the Army confirmed remained current in July. The evaluation identified projectile metal-part production as the limiting factor. The Mesquite facility had produced no conforming projectile parts despite substantial investment.

There is also evidence of a downstream load-assemble-pack gap. Producing more metal components than completed rounds means some available parts are not yet moving through filling, assembly, inspection and acceptance at the same rate.

That matters because it changes the thesis. Energetic materials and environmental permits are not the demonstrated present national bottleneck. They are a possible next bottleneck—one that becomes visible only after manufacturers solve today’s conformity and assembly problems.

The relevant sequence is:

conforming projectile parts → load-assemble-pack throughput → energetic-material supply → chemical utilities and waste systems → commissioning and military acceptance

Developers encounter the chemical gate precisely because they have cleared the more visible manufacturing gate.

A complete shot is a chemical system

A 155mm shell body is not a usable round. The Army defines a complete shot as a fuze, primer, explosively loaded projectile and propelling charge. Increasing output therefore requires several production systems to rise together: projectile machining, load-assemble-pack facilities, explosive fill, propellant, primers, fuzes, inspection and military acceptance. (U.S. Army complete-shot programme)

Energetic materials scale differently from machined metal. TNT, IMX-class fills, nitrocellulose and propellants depend on nitration processes, acid recovery, controlled water systems, air permits, hazardous-waste treatment and explosives-safety infrastructure. A new machine tool can be installed inside an existing factory. A new energetic-material line may require a much larger operating envelope: blast separation, chemical recovery, waste disposal, environmental monitoring, safe startup and lot qualification.

This does not make every permit a bottleneck. It makes chemical infrastructure a sequential dependency. Energetics becomes the pacing constraint only when qualified material supply expands more slowly than conforming projectile and assembly capacity.

That distinction separates strategic importance from current bindingness. The United States clearly needs more resilient TNT, explosive and propellant capacity. Current evidence does not show that this capacity is what limits the marginal completed round today.

The named projects show different stages of relief

The industrial response is already distributed across greenfield construction, existing government plants, brownfield restarts and allied imports.

Graham is the clearest U.S. resilience project. In December 2024, the Army awarded REPKON USA Defense a contract with a ceiling of $435 million to design, build and commission a TNT plant in Graham, Kentucky. The project is intended to restore U.S. TNT production after decades without a domestic node. (U.S. Army Graham award)

The capacity numbers require precision. The Army’s preliminary 2023 market inquiry considered a range of five million to fifteen million pounds per year and a preferred 36-month, outside 48-month construction-and-commissioning period. The awarded procurement describes a five-million-pound annual capability and a four-year design-and-construction base period. Graham is therefore strategically important, but it should not yet be counted as operating supply. (GAO Graham procurement record)

Holston shows what a permit stack actually means

Holston Army Ammunition Plant provides the strongest project-level evidence for the chemical constraint.

BAE Systems operates the government-owned Tennessee explosives facility under a ten-year contract with an $8.8 billion ceiling. The ceiling is procurement authority, not guaranteed revenue, but it shows the scale of the operating relationship. BAE has also described more than $1 billion of Army modernization at Holston, including new nitration and weak-acetic-acid recovery infrastructure. (BAE Holston operating contract)

The plant’s February 2025 environmental assessment makes the industrial mechanism concrete. Expansion involves Clean Air Act and Title V requirements, wastewater controls, hazardous-waste handling and limits on NTO releases into water. The assessment also records RCRA-related delays affecting static-detonation and flashing-furnace alternatives to open burning. (Holston environmental assessment)

This is direct evidence that permitting can delay an energetic-material subsystem. It is not evidence that the delay currently caps national completed-round output.

That is the boundary the analysis must preserve. Environmental systems are neither peripheral paperwork nor automatically the dominant constraint. They are production infrastructure whose importance rises as chemical throughput rises.

Radford Army Ammunition Plant presents the propellant version of the same problem. The Virginia facility produces nitrocellulose and propellants, while Army modernization materials identify water infrastructure as critical. Joint Munitions Command materials describe approximately $715 million of environmental investment, a reduction in open burning and a planned energetic-waste incinerator. The record did not confirm that the incinerator was operating as of the July 2026 review. (Army ammunition-plant modernization)

The closest base rate is faster—and simpler

The closest execution base rate in the available record is the Marion M119A2 propelling-charge facility in Illinois.

The Army awarded the project in September 2023. It produced its first 5,000 charges within eleven months and opened in October 2024 with capacity of up to 33,000 charges per month. (U.S. Army Marion facility)

The similarity is urgent state-backed capacity expansion for a military-qualified ammunition input. The difference is important: Marion is a defined charge-production facility, while Graham is a greenfield TNT chemical complex involving nitration, recovery, environmental controls and bulk-material commissioning.

Marion therefore sets a useful lower-bound execution case, not a direct schedule forecast for Graham. It proves that relevant propelling-charge capacity can enter production quickly. It also weakens any blanket claim that the permit stack necessarily imposes a multi-year delay on every energetic or propellant node.

Europe supplies two additional relief cases. Eurenco inaugurated two large-calibre propellant-powder lines at Bergerac in March 2025, with reported output planned to rise from roughly 1,200 to 1,800 tonnes. The European Commission reported by November 2025 that Chemring Nobel’s Norwegian expansion had completed major construction milestones and installed key equipment. Chemical relief is no longer wholly theoretical. (Reuters on Bergerac)

Existing permitted plants control the near-term bridge

The strongest near-term position belongs to plants that already combine an operating permit, trained workforce, qualified process and logistics network.

Poland’s Nitro-Chem illustrates that advantage. Reuters reported a roughly $310 million agreement to supply 18,000 tonnes of TNT to the U.S. market during 2027–2029. The company reportedly did not need a new production line or additional hiring for the contract. Existing infrastructure can therefore bridge the period before Graham reaches accepted output. (Reuters on Nitro-Chem)

Sweden’s Nora project represents the opposite position. Reuters reported that Sweden’s Land and Environmental Court approved the proposed plant and attributed to the developer a target of 4,500 tonnes per year by 2028. The approval converts a policy objective into a developable project, but capacity and timing remain targets until the plant is built, commissioned and qualified. (Reuters on the Nora project)

The contrast is commercially important. Nitro-Chem can monetize an existing operating base now. Nora and Graham first create construction and commissioning work; recurring material revenue follows only after accepted production begins.

Strategic control does not guarantee high margins

The value pool divides differently across the chain.

Existing permitted producers can capture bulk-material contracts while new capacity remains unavailable. Their advantage comes from immediate deliverability, not merely nameplate capacity. Allied allocation, export policy and logistics may determine how durable that advantage becomes.

Greenfield process and engineering providers capture large, mainly project-based revenue from design, construction and commissioning. Graham’s $435 million ceiling is evidence of a significant spend path, but it does not reveal REPKON’s realized revenue, subcontract split, margin or responsibility for late or off-spec output.

Government-owned, contractor-operated plants create recurring operating relationships. BAE’s positions at Holston and Radford place it inside explosives, propellant, maintenance, modernization and workflow control. The government owns the strategic asset, while the incumbent operator retains process knowledge, safety history and a trained workforce. Those switching costs may create durable control without producing unrestricted pricing power.

Environmental-system suppliers can benefit from acid recovery, wastewater treatment, emissions controls, energetic-waste incineration and compliance work. These systems are technically necessary. Their economics may still resemble competitively procured equipment, engineering or pass-through expenditure rather than scarcity rents.

Qualification and testing form another control point. A chemically valid batch has no complete-shot value until it clears material specifications, lot acceptance and compatibility with downstream assembly. Public records establish that this gate exists but provide little evidence on external testing backlogs, pricing or project-specific qualification schedules.

The clearest public-market exposure in the report is therefore indirect. BAE Systems participates through GOCO plant operation and modernization. Rheinmetall participates through ammunition and powder expansion and broader vertical-integration activity. These positions indicate supply-chain exposure, not an investment conclusion. Government ownership, subsidies and cost-based procurement can absorb strategic value that might otherwise appear as supplier margin.

The bottleneck may migrate without staying long

The central scenario is not a permanent shortage of TNT or propellant. It is a temporary divergence between production layers.

In the base case, metal-part conformity and LAP remain the main U.S. constraints through much of 2027. Marion, Bergerac, Chemring Nobel and Nitro-Chem add relief while Graham advances through construction. Energetics becomes binding only in selected programmes or periods between 2027 and 2029.

A faster migration would require conforming projectile and LAP output to improve while completed-round production remains capped by a named shortage of TNT, IMX, nitrocellulose, propellant or charges. A permit, waste-system or military-qualification delay would then become part of the critical path rather than a supporting cost.

The adverse case is equally credible. Existing allied capacity delivers as contracted. Bergerac and Chemring Nobel ramp successfully. Graham commissions without material environmental or qualification slippage. Official reporting continues to identify projectile parts, fuzes, primers or LAP as the limiting factors. In that outcome, energetics remains strategic infrastructure but never becomes the pacing bottleneck of this cycle.

Relief can also arrive through substitution. Moving from TNT to an IMX formulation may reduce dependence on one material while increasing demand for different precursors, processes and qualification work. The bottleneck changes chemistry rather than disappearing.

What would prove the thesis wrong

The strongest counterargument is that governments are expanding several layers at once, fast enough to prevent a durable upstream constraint.

The United States is investing in projectile parts, LAP, propelling charges, TNT, nitrocellulose and explosives plants. Europe is supporting powder, explosives, shells, missiles, testing and raw materials. Allied suppliers can bridge missing domestic capacity. The system does not need every national node to be self-sufficient at the same moment.

The thesis fails as a pacing-bottleneck argument if completed-round output rises substantially without an official explosive or propellant shortage. It also fails if Graham, Bergerac, Chemring Nobel and other projects convert installed equipment into accepted output on schedule while metal parts, fuzes, primers or LAP remain limiting.

Even confirmation of an energetic constraint would not prove durable commercial rents. Public ownership, government indemnification, grants, internal qualification and negotiated operating fees may keep much of the value with state buyers rather than external suppliers.

What to watch

  • By June 30, 2027: the next official U.S. update names the principal 155mm constraint.
  • By December 31, 2027: completed output exceeds the March 2026 baseline of 36,000 rounds/month.
  • During 2027: Nitro-Chem confirms its first delivery under the 18,000-tonne U.S. agreement.
  • By December 31, 2028: an official record names an energetic input as the limiting factor.
  • By December 31, 2029: Graham produces a publicly acknowledged TNT lot accepted for military use.

The shell bottleneck has not yet moved decisively into the chemical stack. Current evidence still points to projectile conformity and assembly. But the industry is building the conditions for the constraint to migrate.

The decisive signal will not be another factory announcement. It will be a dated production record showing that conforming metal parts and LAP capacity can support more completed rounds, while a named explosive, propellant, environmental or qualification gate prevents them from being made.
